catalog_quote: [p. 32] In any phrase or sentence the word units have easily determined limits, because the penultimate syllable (or rather its nucleus, the vowel,) is relatively longer than all other syllables in the word. Length as a prosodic feature does not appear with grammatical or semantic function in giTonga. ... [p. 84] ... penultimate syllable is noticeably longer than the vowels of any other syllable. Length thus serves as a boundary marker, or signalizer of the word unit. It should be noted that the contrast between long and short vowels diminishes in words in non-final position in a sense group. The contrast is clearest in words in isolation and when in final position in a sentence ... Stress § 1.74 Stress is encountered in several different circumstances in giTonga, which constitute a "characteristic" rather than "semantic" use of this feature. Some speakers combine length and stress as the accent borne by the penultimate syllable of the word unit, but this cannot be accepted as characteristic of giTonga. It is of the nature of an individual idiosyncrasy, and may be a temporary acquisition on the part of ... [p. 85] ... stress on the vowel of the final syllable. Nyimuwone agimbilago eyi [ei] (I saw him walking over there) Womo mule (mur) (He is in there over yonder) ... [p. 4] ... accent (i.e. the penultimate syllable).
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: The word accent of GiTonga is penultimate and its exponent is vowel length: the penultimate vowel of every word is longer than all others and demarcates the word (p. 32: 'the penultimate syllable (or rather its nucleus, the vowel) is relatively longer than all other syllables in the word'; p. 4 glosses 'accent' as 'i.e. the penultimate syllable'). The length contrast is strongest in isolation and sentence-finally and weakens phrase-medially. Dynamic stress is not a regular property of the penult (penult stress co-occurring with length is dismissed as individual idiosyncrasy); length/stress have no lexical or grammatical (contrastive) function. GiTonga is otherwise a tone language (pp. 77-83).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 85: stress falls on the vowel of the FINAL syllable in distal locative demonstratives/adverbs ('over there', 'over yonder': eyi, mule), a 'characteristic' expressive use; sec. 1.75 introduces a further stress use of similar nature (text not visible). Penultimate length contrast diminishes in non-final position within a sense group.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level demarcative accent (every 'word unit' has a long penult, used by Lanham as the criterion for word division, p. 33), but phonetically clearest on words in isolation (citation forms) and sentence-final words; reduced sense-group-medially. Gowlett 2003:617 describes the same feature for Zone S generally as phrase/sentence-final penultimate length-stress in declaratives, absent in interrogatives/exclamatives.
new_statements.identity_note: Lanham 1955 describes GiTonga of Inhambane town and surroundings (glottocode gito1238, ISO toh; he notes some dialect variation, p. 4). Not to be confused with Zambian/Zimbabwean Tonga (tong1318, M64 — Torrend's 'Tonga'), Malawian Tonga (tong1321, N15) or Tsonga/Thonga (tson1249, S53). Gowlett 2003's statement is generic for Guthrie Zone S (minus Lozi), covering S62 GiTonga by inclusion only.

sources.citation: Gowlett, Derek. 2003. Zone S. In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 609-638. London: Routledge. Section 3.6 'Accent/stress', p. 617.
sources.note: Zone-level statement covering GiTonga (S62) by inclusion: 'With the exception of Lozi, Zone S languages have a penultimate length-stress feature which signals the end of a phrase or sentence in declarative sentences. This accent is not used in interrogative and exclamatory sentences.' Also: Zone S languages have two-tone systems with downstep. GiTonga data are cited throughout the chapter but no GiTonga-specific accent statement.

sources.note: Gitonga has lexical tone with a privative H vs toneless (Ø) contrast (minimal pairs, e.g. ɲi-na-róɽ-a 'I will pick up' vs ɲi-na-róɽ-á 'I will become short'; ɽító 'Lito' vs ɽitó 'the voice'), H.H contrasts with H.ꜜH (downstep), and a word-final H spreads onto a following toneless syllable. Penultimate lengthening is realised by vowel duration only (not intensity or pitch), longest in utterance-penult (ratio up to 2.7), intermediate in p-phrase penult, often absent word-internally.
